s0101.literal: His grandfather Xi Zhi was Aide-de-Camp to the Prince of Jin'an of Qi and Administrator of Huainan; he had able administration, and Emperor Wu of Qi repeatedly praised and rewarded him in handwritten edicts.
s0101.idiomatic: His grandfather Xi Zhi had been aide to Qi’s prince of Jin’an and administrator of Huainan, a capable magistrate whom Emperor Wu of Qi repeatedly praised in his own hand.

s0102.literal: His father Jingyan was Liang Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and Minister of Agriculture.
s0102.idiomatic: His father Jingyan had been Liang’s left vice director of the masters of writing and minister of agriculture.

s0103.literal: Shizhi loved learning and had talent for his age.
s0103.idiomatic: Shizhi was studious and had real talent for his day.

s0104.literal: He ranged widely through books and histories, was skilled at literary composition, good at ritual forms, and knew many details of secretariat precedent.
s0104.idiomatic: He read widely in history, wrote well, understood ceremony, and knew secretariat precedent in detail.

s0105.literal: Under Liang he successively served as staff officer in princely households.
s0105.idiomatic: Under Liang he served in several princes’ households as staff officer.

s0106.literal: At the beginning of Shaotai the Founder entered to assist the government and appointed Shizhi Palace Secretariat Attendant-in-Ordinary, in charge of edicts and proclamations.
s0106.idiomatic: When Shaotai began the Founder took power as regent and made Shizhi a palace secretariat attendant-in-ordinary in charge of edicts.

s0107.literal: At that time, after the military disorders, ritual observances were largely missing; when the Founder was Chancellor and received the Nine Bestowals and then the abdication, all the ritual protocols were set by Shizhi.
s0107.idiomatic: After the wars ritual was largely lost; Shizhi drew up the protocols for the Founder’s regency, the Nine Bestowals, and the abdication.

s0108.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate he remained Attendant-in-Ordinary.
s0108.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne Shizhi kept his post as attendant-in-ordinary.

s0109.literal: By nature he was blunt and simple and often at odds with others; though his official rank did not advance, his commission was very weighty, and the proposals he offered all had broad benefit.
s0109.idiomatic: He was blunt and often clashed with others; though his rank scarcely rose, his trust was great and his counsel was always useful.

s0110.literal: When the Founder died, on the sixth day they completed mourning dress; the court ministers together discussed whether the attendants at the late emperor’s spirit seat should wear auspicious or inauspicious garments. Academician Shen Wen’a argued that they should wear auspicious dress.
s0110.idiomatic: When the Founder died, on the sixth day mourning dress was completed. The court debated whether attendants at the late emperor’s spirit seat should wear auspicious or mourning dress. Academician Shen Wen’a argued for auspicious dress.

s0111.literal: Shizhi argued: "Since it is called completing mourning dress, it is fundamentally to prepare the mourning rites; all garments and objects at the spirit couch should be entirely plain white.
s0111.idiomatic: Shizhi argued: "Completing mourning dress means preparing the full mourning rite. Everything at the spirit couch should be plain white.

s0112.literal: Though today there is no office of attendants for the late emperor’s spirit seat, according to when Crown Prince Zhaoming of Liang died, at the completion of mourning dress the attendant officers all wore the coarsest hemp, differing only in that they still wore armor—this may serve as a model.
s0112.idiomatic: There is no formal office of spirit-seat attendants now, but when Liang’s Crown Prince Zhaoming died his attendants at the completion of mourning all wore the coarsest hemp, except that they still wore armor. That is our model.

s0113.literal: I hold that on the sixth day, when mourning dress is completed, those attending the spirit seat must wear hemp mourning.
s0113.idiomatic: On the sixth day, when mourning dress is completed, attendants at the spirit seat should wear hemp mourning.

s0114.literal: " Palace Secretariat Attendant-in-Ordinary Cai Jingli also said: "Though it does not fully accord, according to the fact that for the imperial tomb there are auspicious and inauspicious regalia, and completion of mourning dress has only the inauspicious and not the auspicious, civil and military attendants cannot alone wear jade pendants and sable tails; in feeling and ritual there are two or three points, and they ought to wear coarse hemp.
s0114.idiomatic: " Cai Jingli, palace secretariat attendant-in-ordinary, also said: "The tomb procession has both auspicious and mourning regalia, but completion of mourning dress is mourning only. Civil and military attendants cannot alone wear jade and sable. In ritual feeling they should wear coarse hemp."

s0115.literal: " Palace Secretariat Attendants Jiang Dezao, Xie Qi, and others all agreed with Shizhi’s view.
s0115.idiomatic: Palace secretariat attendants Jiang Dezao, Xie Qi, and others all sided with Shizhi.

s0116.literal: Wen’a argued again: "Checking the Jin and Song tomb protocols: ‘When the spirit carriage and inner coffin descend to the hall, each attendant-in-ordinary reports.’
s0116.idiomatic: Wen’a replied: "The Jin and Song tomb protocols say: ‘When the spirit carriage and inner coffin descend to the hall, each attendant-in-ordinary reports.’

s0117.literal: The protocol for completing mourning dress also says: ‘The spirit carriage and inner coffin accommodate attendant officers and incense and oranges.’
s0117.idiomatic: The protocol for completing mourning dress also says: ‘The spirit carriage and inner coffin accommodate attendant officers, incense, and oranges.’

s0118.literal: Checking again the protocol for the spirit carriage and inner coffin’s advance and halt, it says: ‘Direct attendants at the spirit seat wear auspicious dress and are in the auspicious guard of honor.’
s0118.idiomatic: The protocol for the spirit carriage’s advance and halt says: ‘Direct attendants at the spirit seat wear auspicious dress and stand in the auspicious guard of honor.’

s0119.literal: It also says: ‘Attendants at the inner coffin wear hemp mourning and are in the inauspicious guard of honor.’
s0119.idiomatic: It also says: ‘Attendants at the inner coffin wear hemp mourning and stand in the inauspicious guard of honor.’

s0120.literal: Thus in the hall there are both auspicious and inauspicious attendants.
s0120.idiomatic: So in the hall there are both auspicious and mourning attendants."

s0121.literal: At the time, because the two arguments differed, they submitted a memorial asking Left Vice Director Xu Ling to decide.
s0121.idiomatic: Because the two sides disagreed, they asked left vice director Xu Ling to decide.

s0122.literal: Ling said: "The inner coffin is lodged at the mountain tomb and the spirit couch at the ancestral temple—there is this division, and from it auspicious and inauspicious are verified.
s0122.idiomatic: Ling said: "The inner coffin goes to the tomb and the spirit couch to the ancestral temple. That division itself shows what is auspicious and what is mourning.

s0123.literal: According to the auspicious section of the tomb guard of honor
s0123.idiomatic: In the auspicious section of the tomb guard of honor

s0125.literal: [8] in the [five] ranks, from the dukes and ministers down through those who lead the procession, as well as the tiger guards, musicians, canopy bearers, and chariot attendants—all wear auspicious dress. How could the spirit-seat attendants alone wear hemp mourning?
s0125.idiomatic: [8] in the fifth rank, from dukes and ministers down through guides, tiger guards, musicians, canopy bearers, and chariot attendants—all wear auspicious dress. How could spirit-seat attendants alone wear hemp mourning?

s0127.literal: If one says that dukes, ministers, clerks, and attendants all wear hemp cloth, what difference is there between them and the inner-coffin guard?
s0127.idiomatic: If dukes, ministers, clerks, and attendants all wore hemp, how would they differ from the inner-coffin guard?

s0128.literal: If one says that ritual objects are all auspicious but those who manage affairs are inauspicious, how could one
s0128.idiomatic: If ritual objects are auspicious but those who manage affairs are in mourning, how could one

s0130.literal: [10] [lapels] wear hemp at the lapels yet hold the state canopy, or wear mourning robes yet mount the jade chariot?
s0130.idiomatic: [10] wear hemp at the lapels yet hold the state canopy, or wear mourning robes yet mount the jade chariot?

s0131.literal: I agree with the academician’s view.

s0132.literal: Shizhi argued again: "The left vice director cites the inner coffin lodged at the mountain tomb and the spirit couch at the ancestral temple, saying there must be auspicious and inauspicious sections; completion of mourning dress cannot have the upper part inauspicious. The academician still holds to his former decision, which is ultimately the tomb protocol.
s0132.idiomatic: Shizhi argued again: "The left vice director says the inner coffin goes to the tomb and the spirit couch to the temple, so there must be auspicious and mourning sections, and completion of mourning dress cannot have mourning above. The academician still holds to the tomb rite.

s0133.literal: If when the imperial carriage begins the funeral procession both regalia are set out together, auspicious and inauspicious protocols have from the outset been complete—measured against completion of mourning dress, I am still uneasy.
s0133.idiomatic: When the imperial carriage begins the funeral both regalia are already in place. Measured against completion of mourning dress, I am still uneasy.

s0134.literal: The regulations of mourning rites extend from the Son of Heaven down.
s0134.idiomatic: Mourning regulations extend from the Son of Heaven downward.

s0135.literal: According to Wang Wenhien’s Explanations of Mourning Dress it states: ‘For officials of the third rank, twenty persons attend the spirit.
s0135.idiomatic: Wang Wenhien’s Explanations of Mourning Dress says: ‘For officials of the third rank, twenty persons attend the spirit.

s0136.literal: For the fourth rank down to the scholar’s rites, the number attending the spirit is ten in each case.
s0136.idiomatic: From the fourth rank down to the scholar’s rite, ten attend the spirit in each case.

s0137.literal: All wear white-cloth trousers and jackets and white-silk caps.
s0137.idiomatic: All wear white-cloth trousers and jackets and white-silk caps.

s0138.literal: For inner mourning, female attendants are as numerous as the outer, but they wear the second-grade hemp.
s0138.idiomatic: For inner mourning the women attendants match the men in number but wear second-grade hemp.

s0139.literal: Someone asked: if inner and outer attendants to the spirit are the same, why suddenly is mourning dress different?
s0139.idiomatic: Someone asked: if inner and outer attendants are the same, why is mourning dress different?

s0140.literal: The answer was: if one follows the rites of ruler and minister, then the outer attendants wear the coarsest cut and the inner the second grade.
s0140.idiomatic: The answer was: by ruler-and-minister rites the outer attendants wear the coarsest cut and the inner the second grade.

s0141.literal: In recent generations there have been many troubles, and rites have been reduced as affairs required.
s0141.idiomatic: Recent ages have seen many troubles, and rites were cut to fit the times.

s0142.literal: Below the rank of feudal lord, ministers and clerks were slight; as for attendance, most came from voluntary attachment. The relation of ruler and minister was not complete, and the expense of hemp caps was in fact lacking; therefore they kept their ordinary dress and only changed the cap.
s0142.idiomatic: Below feudal lords, officials were humble and attendants mostly volunteers. Ruler-minister form was incomplete and hemp caps too costly, so they kept ordinary dress and only changed the cap.

s0143.literal: Women who attended were all low servants; the way of lord and concubine was pure, and therefore their dress and insignia were complete.
s0143.idiomatic: Women attendants were low servants; lord and concubine stood apart, so their dress was complete.’

s0144.literal: The statutes of our dynasty are still not so; from this one infers that the coarsest hemp should be worn.
s0144.idiomatic: Our dynasty’s code is not like that. From this one infers coarse hemp.

s0145.literal: Where there are attendants to the spirit, it is like attendants at the seat; once they wear the white cap, by principle there can be no colored dress.
s0145.idiomatic: Spirit attendants are like seat attendants; in white caps they cannot wear colored dress.

s0146.literal: Moreover the Liang protocols for Crown Prince Zhaoming still exist today; these two texts are clear evidence and may serve as a settled standard.
s0146.idiomatic: Liang’s protocols for Crown Prince Zhaoming still survive. Those two texts are clear proof and a settled standard.

s0147.literal: Moreover rites arise from human feeling and may be adjusted in message.
s0147.idiomatic: Rites arise from feeling and may be adjusted in practice.

s0148.literal: Whenever anyone has a bereavement, once the spirit couch and offering tables are set out, curtains and spirit screens are hung, [11] ordinary observances are changed, and reed mats and grass huts are the inauspicious rite.
s0148.idiomatic: When anyone mourns, once the spirit couch and tables are set out and curtains hung, ordinary life changes; reed mats and grass huts are the mourning rite.

s0149.literal: Within the hall, kin and guests all come; in coarse hemp of various grades they take their places weeping in ranks; black caps do not pay condolence calls—all are plain dress.
s0149.idiomatic: Within the hall kin and guests gather in hemp of every grade, weeping in ranks. Black caps do not call—all wear plain dress.

s0150.literal: How could one see students and old retainers hurrying in silk and gauze, with concubines left and right in red and purple mingled?
s0150.idiomatic: Who could see students and retainers rushing about in silk, with concubines in red and purple at their sides?

s0151.literal: How much more when the realm is in deep mourning and feeling under Heaven is one; the three armies in plain white—the regulation of dress is uniform.
s0151.idiomatic: How much more when the realm is in deep mourning and all under Heaven feels as one, and the three armies wear plain white in a single regulation of dress.

s0152.literal: Thus a thousand gates open at dawn—not whitewash on the vermilion gate; the hundred officials arrive and stop—coarse dress replaces the vermilion sash; yet gleaming gold stands in the ranks and sounding jade marks the procession. Sought in the heart, it is plainly unsatisfying; measured against the ritual canon, there is even less precedent.
s0152.idiomatic: Yet a thousand gates open at dawn without whitewash on the vermilion gate; the hundred officials arrive in coarse dress instead of vermilion sashes, while gold gleams in the ranks and jade sounds in procession. In the heart it cannot satisfy; by the ritual canon there is no precedent.

s0153.literal: How can the rites of completing mourning dress be likened to the tomb protocol?
s0153.idiomatic: How can completion of mourning dress be likened to the tomb rites?

s0154.literal: When burial has begun and ended, there are therefore auspicious and inauspicious protocols—what is called completing mourning dress is fundamentally completing the mourning rite. Inside and outside, the hundred offices all change to auspicious appearance; if the spirit-seat attendants alone do not, what is called completing mourning dress?
s0154.idiomatic: When burial is finished there are auspicious and mourning protocols. Completing mourning dress means completing the mourning rite. All offices inside and out change to auspicious dress—if spirit-seat attendants alone do not, what is completion of mourning?

s0155.literal: If there are no spirit-seat attendants, so be it; if there are, they must wear hemp mourning.
s0155.idiomatic: If there are no spirit-seat attendants, so be it; if there are, they must wear hemp mourning."

s0156.literal: Xie Qi argued: "The spirit couch is lodged at the ancestral temple and the inner coffin at the mountain tomb—this is truly as the left vice director said.
s0156.idiomatic: Xie Qi argued: "The spirit couch goes to the temple and the inner coffin to the tomb, as the left vice director said.

s0157.literal: But in the tomb guard of honor auspicious and inauspicious are both provided; those who follow the spirit carriage do not change dress, while those who follow the inner coffin all wear hemp cloth.
s0157.idiomatic: But the tomb guard has both auspicious and mourning sections. Those who follow the spirit carriage keep their dress; those who follow the inner coffin all wear hemp.

s0158.literal: Down to the scholar’s rites all follow this regulation—this is itself the tomb protocol and does not concern completion of mourning dress.
s0158.idiomatic: Down to the scholar’s rite the rule is the same. That is the tomb rite, not completion of mourning dress.

s0159.literal: Now we call the inner coffin and spirit screen both on the western steps ‘completing mourning dress,’ yet there is no guard of honor—only from clerks and attendants up to dukes and ministers, within the four seas, all must wear hemp mourning.
s0159.idiomatic: Now the inner coffin and spirit screen both stand on the western steps and we call it completing mourning dress, yet there is no guard of honor—only that from clerks to dukes, throughout the realm, all must wear hemp.

s0160.literal: According to when Crown Prince Zhaoming of Liang died, which is roughly the established example—how could common scholars and people all wear the heavy grade, while attendants-in-ordinary down to the martial guards, who are the nearest officers, on the contrary sound jade and twist azure, no different from ordinary auspicious days?
s0160.idiomatic: When Liang’s Crown Prince Zhaoming died is the established example. How could every commoner wear the heavy grade while attendants-in-ordinary down to the martial guards—the nearest officers—wore jade and azure no differently from an ordinary auspicious day?

s0161.literal: The left vice director, pushing the matter of the tomb, in my humble view perhaps differs from completion of mourning dress.
s0161.idiomatic: The left vice director treats it as a tomb matter; I think that may differ from completion of mourning dress.

s0162.literal: If on that day the spirit-seat attendants, civil and military, were not different, then those who attend the spirit—the chief clerks, heralds, runners, and responders to edicts—should all likewise not change.
s0162.idiomatic: If on that day spirit-seat attendants, civil and military alike, were unchanged, then chief clerks, heralds, runners, and responders to edicts who attend the spirit should likewise not change."

s0163.literal: Cai Jingli argued again: "The office of spirit-seat attendants originally came from the five hundred; on that day, though they wore mourning dress and dwelt in the mourning hut, they were still in their original department and were led up to ascend the hall—how could they change to sable and jade?
s0163.idiomatic: Cai Jingli argued again: "Spirit-seat attendants came from the five hundred. That day they wore mourning dress and dwelt in the mourning hut but still belonged to their offices and were led up to the hall—how could they change to sable and jade?

s0164.literal: If other officials were specially assigned to fill the ranks of insignia, then on that day there would be some who had not completed mourning dress.
s0164.idiomatic: If other officers were drafted to fill the insignia ranks, then on that day some would not have completed mourning dress.

s0165.literal: The tomb has its own debate on auspicious and inauspicious; completion of mourning dress is inauspicious and not auspicious—still following the former view, I agree with Attendant Liu.
s0165.idiomatic: The tomb has its own auspicious-and-mourning debate. Completion of mourning dress is mourning, not auspicious. I still follow the former view and agree with Attendant Liu."

s0166.literal: Dezao argued again: "I hold that on the day of the ancestral burial, when beginning and end are forever complete, high officials receive posthumous honors and must display grace and glory; there is an auspicious guard of honor, and I fear the meaning lies here. Private families imitated it, and thus it became custom.
s0166.idiomatic: Dezao argued again: "On the day of ancestral burial, when the rite is forever complete, high officials receive posthumous honors and display grace. The auspicious guard may come from that. Private families imitated it and it became custom.

s0167.literal: Upper dress fundamentally changes from auspicious to inauspicious; by principle one should not still wear silk gauze.
s0167.idiomatic: Upper dress should change from auspicious to mourning; by principle one should not still wear silk gauze.

s0168.literal: Attendant Liu cited General Wang’s mourning protocol and checked the Liang Zhaoming precedent—this clear evidence is already established. The academician and left vice director each exhausted their views; since no proof was taken, inquiry must go further. It should be put to the eight ministers, the household tutor of the heir apparent, the minister of rites, the censor-in-chief
s0168.idiomatic: Attendant Liu cited General Wang’s mourning protocol and the Liang Zhaoming precedent—clear proof already in hand. The academician and left vice director each stated his view; since no decision was reached, inquiry should go further—to the eight ministers, the heir apparent’s tutor, the minister of rites, the censor-in-chief

s0170.literal: [12] and the household tutors and general attendants Yuan Shu, Zhang Zhong, Zhou Hongzheng, Hongrang, Shen Jiong, and Kong Huan.
s0170.idiomatic: [12] and the household tutors and general attendants Yuan Shu, Zhang Zhong, Zhou Hongzheng, Hongrang, Shen Jiong, and Kong Huan."

s0171.literal: At that time the eight ministers and below all requested: "Considering the group discussions and weighing old protocol, the Liang protocols for completing mourning dress at Crown Prince Zhaoming’s death exist in clear text today and suffice as a standard.
s0171.idiomatic: The eight ministers and below all submitted: "Weighing the discussions and old protocol, Liang’s protocols for completing mourning dress at Crown Prince Zhaoming’s death survive in clear text and suffice as standard.

s0172.literal: On the day of completing mourning dress, attendant officers by principle cannot still follow auspicious rites.
s0172.idiomatic: On the day of completing mourning dress, attendant officers cannot follow auspicious rites.

s0173.literal: That burial rites are divided into auspicious sections is a matter of the time of the mountain tomb and does not concern the day of completing mourning dress.
s0173.idiomatic: Burial rites divide into auspicious sections at the tomb; that does not concern the day of completing mourning dress.

s0174.literal: I hold that Attendant Liu’s view is acceptable in the matter.
s0174.idiomatic: We hold that Attendant Liu’s view is acceptable."

s0175.literal: Ling answered again: "Old and ill, I lie with the coverlet up to my chin and cannot say much. Men of old who disputed often became objects of resentment; Fu Xuan was blamed in the Jin age and Wang Shang fell into trouble in Han—I respectfully seal my lips thrice and honor your high command.
s0175.idiomatic: Ling answered again: "Old and ill, I can say little. Men of old who disputed often bred resentment; Fu Xuan was blamed in Jin and Wang Shang fell in Han. I seal my lips thrice and honor your command.

s0176.literal: If by any chance I do not die, I may yet speak further and, with the court worthies, discuss again in detail.
s0176.idiomatic: If by chance I do not die, I may yet speak and discuss the matter again with the court."

s0177.literal: Wen’a still held to his view; the assembly could not decide, so they fully recorded both arguments and submitted them, following Shizhi’s view.
s0177.idiomatic: Wen’a still held to his view. The assembly could not decide, recorded both arguments, submitted them, and followed Shizhi’s view.

s0178.literal: Soon he was transferred to Minister Herald, his post as Attendant-in-Ordinary unchanged.
s0178.idiomatic: Soon he was made minister herald, keeping his post as attendant-in-ordinary.

s0179.literal: In the first year of Tianjia he was dismissed for an offense.
s0179.idiomatic: In Tianjia year one he was dismissed for an offense.

s0180.literal: Earlier, Emperor Wen had ordered Shizhi to compile the imperial diary from the autumn of Yongding year two to the winter of Tianjia year one, ten scrolls.
s0180.idiomatic: Earlier Emperor Wen had ordered Shizhi to compile the imperial diary from autumn of Yongding year two through winter of Tianjia year one—ten scrolls.

s0181.literal: He was raised as Palace Secretariat Attendant-in-Ordinary and again put in charge of edicts and proclamations.
s0181.idiomatic: He was recalled as palace secretariat attendant-in-ordinary and again put in charge of edicts.

s0182.literal: In the first year of Tiankang, when Emperor Wen was ill, Shizhi together with Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Dao Zhongju and others entered to attend with medicine.
s0182.idiomatic: In Tiankang year one, when Emperor Wen fell ill, Shizhi with vice director of the masters of writing Dao Zhongju and others entered to tend him with medicine.

s0183.literal: When Emperor Wen died, he received the testamentary charge in advance.
s0183.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen died, Shizhi had already received the deathbed charge.

s0184.literal: When Emperor Xuan was Director of the Masters of Writing and entered to assist, in the first year of Guangda, Shizhi together with Zhongju and others sent Attendant Yin Buniu with a forged order telling Emperor Xuan to return to the Eastern Mansion; the affair was discovered and at the northern prison he was granted death.
s0184.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan was director of the masters of writing and regent, in Guangda year one Shizhi with Zhongju and others sent attendant Yin Buniu with a forged order telling Emperor Xuan to return to the Eastern Mansion. The plot was exposed and he was granted death in the northern prison.

s0185.literal: Xie Qi was a man of Shanyin in Kuaiji.
s0185.idiomatic: Xie Qi was from Shanyin in Kuaiji.

s0186.literal: His father Da was a Liang Erudite of the Imperial Academy.
s0186.idiomatic: His father Da was a Liang erudite of the imperial academy.

s0187.literal: Qi in youth was quick-witted, loved learning, and was praised in the Liang age.
s0187.idiomatic: Qi was quick-witted as a youth, loved learning, and won praise under Liang.

s0188.literal: He was Lang of the Ministry of Revenue in the Masters of Writing and Magistrate of Shanyin.
s0188.idiomatic: He was a revenue clerk in the masters of writing and magistrate of Shanyin.

s0189.literal: When Hou Jing rebelled, Qi wandered in Dongyang.
s0189.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled, Qi took refuge in Dongyang.

s0190.literal: When Jing was pacified, he attached himself to Zhang Biao.
s0190.idiomatic: After Jing was suppressed he joined Zhang Biao.

s0191.literal: When Biao was in Wu commandery and Kuaiji, he entrusted all miscellaneous affairs to Qi.
s0191.idiomatic: When Biao held Wu and Kuaiji he entrusted all routine affairs to Qi.

s0192.literal: Whenever Biao went on campaign, he always left Qi to supervise the commandery and manage subsequent affairs.
s0192.idiomatic: Whenever Biao campaigned he left Qi to supervise the commandery and handle affairs behind him.

s0193.literal: When Biao was defeated, the Founder drew Qi into confidential planning and made him Acting Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
s0193.idiomatic: When Biao was defeated the Founder drew Qi into confidential planning and made him acting right vice director of the masters of writing.

s0194.literal: At that time campaigns were frequent and grain stores often lacked; wherever Qi took charge of affairs he was deeply known and favored.
s0194.idiomatic: Campaigns were frequent and grain stores often empty; wherever Qi managed affairs he won deep trust.

s0195.literal: In the first year of Yongding he was made Attendant of the Yellow Gate and Palace Secretariat Attendant-in-Ordinary, still acting right vice director as before.
s0195.idiomatic: In Yongding year one he was made attendant of the yellow gate and palace secretariat attendant-in-ordinary, still acting right vice director.

s0196.literal: In the second year of Tianjia he died; he was posthumously made Regular Attendant of Scattered Cavalry.
s0196.idiomatic: In Tianjia year two he died and was posthumously made regular attendant of scattered cavalry.

s0197.literal: Qi’s younger brother Qiao was devoted to learning and was a Confucian master of his age.
s0197.idiomatic: Qi’s younger brother Qiao was devoted to learning and a leading Confucian of the age.

s0198.literal: The historian says: When the Founder opened the foundation and created the enterprise, quelling disaster and disorder, martial fierceness indeed established his achievement, but literary writing also displayed its power.
s0198.idiomatic: The historian says: When the Founder raised the dynasty and quelled chaos, martial prowess won his achievement, but literary men also played their part.

s0199.literal: [13] Zhao Zhili and Cai Jingli early recognized and attached themselves to him; they were ministers in the founding structure.
s0199.idiomatic: [13] Zhao Zhili and Cai Jingli recognized him early and helped build the state.

s0200.literal: Liu Shizhi ranged widely and knew much, yet was dark about timely change; though he wished to preserve integrity and righteousness, in the end he fell to extreme punishment—this was lack of wisdom.
s0200.idiomatic: Liu Shizhi was broadly learned but blind to the moment; though he wished to keep his integrity, he ended on the execution ground—this was folly.
